cards.title: The spotlight effect: fewer people noticed
cards.body:
You trip on the stairs, say something awkward in class, or show up with a bad haircut, and it feels like everyone noticed. They mostly didn't. Psychologists call this the spotlight effect: we overestimate how much attention other people pay to our appearance and our mistakes.

The classic demonstration came from Thomas Gilovich and colleagues in 2000. Students walked into a room wearing a T-shirt with Barry Manilow's face on it, which they found embarrassing. They guessed that about half the people in the room would notice the shirt. In reality, only about a quarter did.

The reason is simple: everyone else is busy starring in their own movie. You are the centre of your attention, not theirs. Knowing this makes it easier to ask the question, take the shot, or try the new thing.
cards.example: In a seminar you ask a question you worry is obvious. Afterwards, ask a friend whether they remember it. Odds are they barely do, because they were thinking about their own question. Try one small test this week: speak up once where you'd normally stay quiet.
cards.takeaway: Everyone is the star of their own movie, not an audience for yours.

cards.title: Stagflation: the decade the Phillips curve broke
cards.body:
In 1958 the economist A. W. Phillips showed that, in Britain, periods of low unemployment tended to come with faster wage growth. Policymakers soon read it as a menu: accept a bit more inflation and you could buy lower unemployment.

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued in the late 1960s that the trade-off was only temporary. Once workers and firms expect higher inflation, they build it into wages and prices, and unemployment drifts back to its natural rate, now with more inflation baked in.

The 1970s proved them right. Oil shocks and entrenched expectations brought double-digit inflation alongside rising unemployment in both Canada and the United States, a combination dubbed stagflation. Breaking it took brutal rate hikes and a deep recession in the early 1980s. The lasting lesson: inflation expectations are what central banks fight hardest to anchor.
cards.example: In 1981 the US Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker pushed its policy rate to around 20%, and the Bank of Canada's rate also topped 20% that year. Inflation fell sharply over the next few years, but unemployment in both countries climbed above 10% in the 1982 recession.
cards.takeaway: You can't buy lasting low unemployment with inflation; expectations catch up.

cards.title: Why the sky is blue and sunsets are red
cards.body:
Sunlight looks white but contains every colour. As it passes through the atmosphere, it bounces off nitrogen and oxygen molecules far smaller than the light's wavelength. This is Rayleigh scattering, and its strength rises steeply as wavelength gets shorter, roughly with the inverse fourth power.

That makes blue light, with its short wavelength, scatter around five to six times more than red. Look at any patch of sky away from the sun and you're seeing blue light that has been bounced toward your eyes from every direction.

Why not violet, which is even shorter? The sun emits less of it, some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset, light travels through far more air to reach you, so most of the blue is scattered away before it arrives, leaving the oranges and reds.
cards.example: Compare blue light at about 450 nanometres with red at about 700. The ratio is 700 / 450 ≈ 1.56, and 1.56 to the fourth power is about 5.9, so blue scatters nearly six times as strongly. Next clear evening, notice how the sky overhead stays blue while the horizon near the sun turns orange.
cards.takeaway: Short wavelengths scatter most: blue by day, red when light crosses more air.

cards.title: Rest longer between sets to grow more
cards.body:
Short rest periods feel hardcore, but for building muscle and strength they usually cost you. When you rest only a minute, you start the next set still fatigued, so you complete fewer reps with the same weight. Over a workout that means less total work, and total work is a main driver of growth.

A 2016 study by Brad Schoenfeld and colleagues had trained men follow the same program with either one-minute or three-minute rests. The three-minute group gained more strength and, on several measures, more muscle thickness.

A practical rule: rest two to three minutes on big compound lifts like squats, bench and rows, and one to two minutes on smaller isolation work like curls and lateral raises. If you're short on time, pair exercises that don't compete, like a press and a row, and alternate between them.
cards.example: This week on bench press, time your rests with your phone: a full 2.5 minutes between sets. If you normally get 8, 6 and 5 reps with 70 kg on short rests, see whether you can hold 8, 8 and 7 instead. Those extra reps are extra growth stimulus.
cards.takeaway: Rest long enough on big lifts that every set is a quality set.

cards.title: Razor and blades: cheap to start, costly to keep
cards.body:
Some of the most profitable businesses sell their main product at little or no profit and make their money on what you must keep buying. Think inkjet printers and ink cartridges, coffee machines and pods, or game consoles and games.

The model works when three things hold. The upfront product must lock you into a consumable or add-on. The consumable must be bought repeatedly at a healthy margin. And switching away must be annoying or costly, through proprietary designs, patents or a library you've built up.

For an investor, this changes how you read the numbers. A segment showing thin margins may be the deliberate cost of acquiring customers, while the real value sits in the recurring stream. The key question is how durable the lock-in is, because if cheap compatible refills arrive, the whole model can unravel.
cards.example: Video game consoles have often launched at or below cost, with the platform owner earning a fee on each game sold and on online subscriptions. So the number to watch isn't console margin but how much each console owner spends on games and subscriptions over the console's life.
cards.takeaway: Look past the product on the shelf to the stream it locks in.

cards.title: The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel
cards.body:
Most finance books teach you what to do. Morgan Housel's 2020 book is about why people, including smart ones, don't do it. Its argument is that doing well with money depends less on intelligence and more on behaviour: patience, humility, and knowing when you have enough.

The book is a series of short chapters, each built around one story and one idea, which makes it ideal for reading in small sessions. Housel covers why compounding is so counterintuitive, why rare tail events drive most outcomes, and why saving without a specific goal is still worth it.

For someone heading toward the buy-side, it's a useful counterweight to spreadsheets. Valuation tells you what something is worth; this book explains why markets, clients and you yourself will so often act differently.
cards.example: Start with chapter 1, No One's Crazy, which argues that everyone's financial decisions make sense given their own experiences. It's short, and it changes how you interpret other investors' seemingly irrational choices.
cards.takeaway: Wealth is mostly a behaviour problem, not a knowledge problem.

quiz.question: In Gilovich's T-shirt study, what did the participants get wrong?
options: They underestimated how many people would notice the shirt
They thought the shirt was more fashionable than observers did
They overestimated how many people would notice the shirt
They forgot which shirt they were wearing
quiz.explanation: Wearers guessed about half the room would notice; only about a quarter did. We overestimate how much others watch us.

quiz.question: According to Friedman and Phelps, why does the Phillips curve trade-off fade over time?
options: Workers and firms come to expect the higher inflation and build it into wages and prices
Central banks always raise rates when unemployment falls
Oil prices eventually rise and offset the effect
Governments stop measuring unemployment accurately
quiz.explanation: Once higher inflation is expected, it is priced into wages and prices, so unemployment returns to its natural rate with inflation left higher.

quiz.question: Why does the sky near the setting sun look orange and red?
options: The sun emits more red light in the evening
Red light scatters more strongly than blue
Clouds absorb blue light near dusk
Light passes through much more air, so most blue is scattered away before reaching you
quiz.explanation: At sunset the light's path through the atmosphere is far longer, so short blue wavelengths are scattered out, leaving longer red and orange ones.

quiz.question: Why do longer rests between heavy sets tend to build more muscle?
options: They keep heart rate higher
They let you complete more reps per set, increasing total work
They burn more calories per session
They reduce how much protein you need
quiz.explanation: Starting each set less fatigued means more reps at the same weight, and more total work drives more growth.

quiz.question: A printer maker's hardware segment shows near-zero margins. Under a razor-and-blades model, what matters most to analyse?
options: The cost of shipping printers
How quickly printer prices fall
The number of printer models offered
How durable the ink lock-in is against cheaper compatible cartridges
quiz.explanation: The printer is the customer-acquisition cost; the value is in recurring ink sales, which only last if customers stay locked in.

quiz.question: What is the central argument of The Psychology of Money?
options: Financial success depends more on behaviour than on intelligence
Index funds always beat active managers
Budgeting apps are the key to building wealth
You need advanced maths to invest well
quiz.explanation: Housel argues that patience, humility and knowing when you have enough matter more than technical skill.
